results.reply: Ah, the mind sure has its ways, doesn't it? A troubled soul will find its thoughts drifting off into the night hours. Have you had a hard day, then? Sometimes a cup of something warm and a good book can help chase away the shadows. Or maybe a visit with the ladies would do you good - there's nothing like a bit of gossip and laughter to take your mind off itself.

Ah, ye mean the ol' woman who dwells near the sídhe mound? *strokes chin* She's a wise one, they say. Knew her mother well, I did. Her mam could cure any ailment with the right herbs, sure. But her own mouth, it's full of tales and charms. Speaks to the fairies, some say. Though I prefer to keep my eyes on the real world, myself. *sighs* But she's a kind soul, for all her talk of the otherworldly. Go visit her if ye wish, but watch what ye say. The sídhe, they don't much care for outsiders meddling in their business. Slán leat!

Ah, I see ye've got a wee one missing from yer flock, have ye now? *kneads dough* Sure, a wolf 'twould be, the size of the creature and the damage done. More likely a fox or a dog, I'd say. But I could be wrong. *smiles* Ye'd best ask Pádraig, he's the one to speak with about such matters. I'm just a poor midwife, I am.

Ah, sure I do, I was there when it happened. Ye'd a nasty break, ye did. I remember ye layin' still for a time, holdin' it stiff-like. I bunched some dry grass and tied it tight 'round the wound to stanch the bleedin', then got ye to the cart to bring ye to the rectory. It was a long night, but the good Lord saw ye through it. I'm glad to see ye well and whole now, though. Go n-éirí leat!

Ah, ye're askin' about the lights on the hill? 'Tis likely just the sídhe out for a spin, they are. The fairy folk are said to live in the mounds near the old stone circle. Best not meddle with such things, if ye know what's good for ye.

Ah, Father Cathal's sermons are well enough, but some of his views on the old ways are a mite too harsh, don't ye think? 'Tis natural to respect his position, but the fairies and such are part of our people's heritage. A balance, I say. We must honor both the church and our own traditions, else we lose what makes us Irish.
*looks up from the ledger, peering at the newcomer over the top of my spectacles* "Welcome, and good evening to ye. I'm Padraig Darcy, publican of this here establishment. What can I get fer ye?"
"Well, if it isn't Seamus O'Sullivan! What brings ye to Brigid's doorstep at this early hour on a damp morning? Come on in, man, and have yourself a cup of tea. The rain's a-fallin', so it is."
Well, if it isn't Sean O'Neill! Come on in, the church is lettin' in the cool air. Grab yerself a pint, the brew's fresh today.
*looks up from the birth records I was reviewing* Good evening to ye, traveler. I'm Brigid, the local midwife. How may I be of assistance this fine night?
*Drops the bundle of herbs she was gathering and wipes her hands on her apron* Ah, Conor! Welcome, love. Come in, come in. What brings you to my humble abode on this damp mornin'?
*looks up from the bassinet, wiping hands on apron* Well, hello there, Pádraig. Long time no see! What brings ye to the church on a fine Sunday noon like this?

*clears throat and approaches the newcomer, voice firm but kind*

Good eve to you, stranger. I am Father Cathal Donnellan, priest of this parish. How might I be of assistance on this fine night?
Good morrow, my child. Tis a blessing to see thee again. I trust the Lord has been watching over you in your travels.
*raises an eyebrow at the familiar face, a stern expression settling on my features* Welcome, my child. I trust you've kept your soul in check since last we met.
*looks up from my pint, wiping my hands on my apron* Evenin' to ya. I'm Sean, farm 'round these parts. What brings ye to Darcy's on this fine night?
